claims.text: The fields are watered with 'fossil' water dating to the last Ice Age; aquifers filled about 20,000 years ago, buried deep
As recently as 1986 there was little to no agriculture in the Wadi As-Sirhan Basin
Fields are about one kilometer across and use center-pivot irrigation (sprinkler rotating about a central pivot)
Net imports of 500,000 t (1980) turned into net exports of more than 2,000,000 t of wheat in 1992
Water is pumped from deep underground aquifers
Aquifers are not recharged; rainfall averages 100-200 mm a year; groundwater is a nonrenewable resource
Saudi Arabia ended its domestic wheat production program by the beginning of 2016 (decree 335 of 2007); main reason: water depletion
Many farmers switched from wheat to forage crops such as alfalfa, which consume three times the water of wheat
In 2016 hydrologists predicted pumping would be feasible for only about another 50 years
Development was largely financed by the Saudi government's oil revenues

observations.text: 1987-04-10: no fields in the hook and core views; 2000/2008/2015/2025: dense center-pivot grids (same grid, same season)
Green area in the stack AOI on the April dates: ~7 km2 (1987), ~629 (2000), ~1016 (2008), ~1268 (2015), ~980 (2025)
observations.status: observation from a crude color threshold on single dates - NOT published, not spoken

inferences.text: The 2015->2025 drop in green area is NOT interpreted (single spring date per year; crop cycles and fallow vary)

excluded: Arizona / Fondomonte (Saudi-owned alfalfa farm, leases ended 2023-24): verified by the Arizona Governor's office, but no visual proof on this grid -> WEAK_PROOF, removed
'The circles stayed green' after 2016: single-date imagery shows ~23% less green in 2025 than 2015 -> could mislead, removed
Number of fields / exact area: only my own threshold estimate -> not published
Town names in frame (not verified against a gazetteer) -> not labelled
Saudi reintroduction of some local wheat purchases after 2019 (not checked) -> no claim about present-day crops
'Fossil water 20,000 years' is NASA's figure for the aquifers; no age range beyond that
